fulltext: IT之家 10 月 4 日消息，特斯拉的 FSD（监督版）今年取得了长足进展：业务向欧洲市场拓展，商用无人驾驶 Robotaxi 也正式落地。不过即便是忠实使用者也清楚，这套系统依旧存在若干长期未能解决的短板。车主反馈最多的两大痛点集中在路线规划与破损路面问题：导航会莫名其妙绕路；FSD 还会径直开过容易扎破轮胎的坑洼路面。
好在这两大问题很快就有望得到修复。Shopify 高管法尔汉 · 塔瓦尔（Farhan Thawar）在 X 平台发帖称赞 FSD v14.3.10 版本，同时也提到破损的沥青路面以及顽固的导航选路逻辑仍是他使用过程当中最大的困扰。
特斯拉 AI 团队首席软件工程师菲尔 · 段（Phil Duan）直接对此作出回复，确认“针对这两方面的改进即将上线。”
IT之家注意到，自动避让路面坑洼是用户呼声最高的功能之一，特斯拉自 2019 年起就已经对此作出过承诺。近期埃隆 · 马斯克也表示坑洼避让功能很快就会正式推出；自今年春季 FSD v14.3 版本开始，特斯拉更是已经在版本更新说明中将该项功能列为待上线改进项。
现阶段的版本偶尔已经可以观察到类似效果。一名测试人员使用 FSD v14.2.2.5 时录下一段视频：车辆行驶时会微调位置，让开裂的路面坑洼刚好处于两侧车轮之间安全通过。但目前尚无法确认神经网络究竟是识别出了坑洼，还只是对一处无法判定的路面异常做出反应；并且该行为在近期各个 FSD 版本当中表现并不稳定。
一旦特斯拉正式推出坑洼避让，这种偶尔出现的避险动作就会转变为稳定可靠的行驶逻辑。以后不再需要驾驶员手动接管来保护轮毂、保障乘坐舒适性，FSD 可以实时识别破损路面，平稳转向绕开坑洼。
导航逻辑同样会迎来大规模重构。虽然 FSD 处理变道、转向的表现尚可，但车主经常吐槽整体选路逻辑：系统总是固执地选择奇怪的支路绕行，而不是沿用车主日常通勤习惯的路线。
特斯拉的解决思路是让 FSD 学习用户的日常驾驶习惯。系统分析驾驶员人工介入的操作，把用户手动选择车道、轻打方向盘的操作当作训练反馈。如果你总是无视导航规划的绕行路线，坚持走自己偏好的高速出口或者城市地面道路，后续出行时 FSD 就会记住这一偏好，不再和驾驶者“较劲抢方向盘”。该新功能建立在特斯拉此前上线的「偏好路线」（Preferred Routes）特性的基础之上。
除此之外，这套学习机制还会延伸至终点停车环节。后续版本的 FSD 将会学习你的停车习惯：记录你是习惯倒车驶入自家车道、紧贴车库墙体留出人行空间，还是停车时与高大路沿保持更远距离。完成学习之后，车辆在自动泊车时就会尽量模仿这些个人习惯。
除坑洼感知与更智能的路线规划以外，特斯拉还正在把 Grok 直接整合进 FSD 的整套系统。驾驶员不再需要点击屏幕菜单；很快就可以使用自然语音直接下达自动驾驶指令，例如要求车辆在某个路口转弯、停放到指定位置，或是临时更改行驶路线。再加上已经上线的自动避险功能 —— 该功能可以在人工驾驶状态下重新激活 FSD 辅助避险。看得出来，特斯拉当下正在紧锣密鼓迭代 FSD。
坑洼避让最初写进了 v14.3 版本更新说明当中，但目前尚不清楚这项升级究竟会随近期的小版本补丁推送，还是等到 FSD v15 架构才正式亮相。FSD v15 预计会带来一次重大神经网络升级，参数量达到 100 亿。无论上线节奏如何，让车辆学会避让路面坑洼、记住车主偏爱的通行道路，都将会让日常自动驾驶通勤的体验顺滑不少。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 4 日消息，特斯拉首席执行官埃隆 · 马斯克于当地时间周六透露，奥斯汀地区的无人驾驶出租车（Robotaxi）运营结束时间将由晚间 22 点延长至 23 点。同时他提到，研发团队一直致力于攻克一个相当隐蔽棘手的问题。
“我们目前着力解决的核心问题，就是避免在夜间视线不佳的情况下碾过宠物。”马斯克在 X 平台发帖写道，“直白地说，就是要防止在黑暗环境当中，灰色的小猫跑到灰色沥青路面上时发生事故。”
历经多年延期之后，特斯拉的无人驾驶出租车已于去年在奥斯汀投入试点运营。自那以后，特斯拉逐步扩大服务范围，覆盖奥斯汀、得克萨斯州其他城市以及佛罗里达州。
特斯拉的 Cybercab 依靠“摄像头视觉以及各类传感器”完成环境感知与行驶导航。在车辆使用手册当中特斯拉也写明：光照不足的环境，包括夜间没有路灯或者照明很差的道路，会限制摄像头输出精准视觉信息的能力。
猫狗这类动物的行动难以预判，会突然窜冲到车道上，相比常规通行车流而言属于更高风险的道路目标。
周六马斯克这条帖子下有网友留言，马斯克在回复当中提出，可以借助 AI 辅助摄像头处理，以此改善夜间识别能力。
“由人工智能完成光子计数分析之后，可见光摄像头在黑暗环境下也可以拥有很不错的识别效果。”他表示。
美国国家公路交通安全管理局（NHTSA）正在针对特斯拉 FSD 的摄像头感知系统展开调查，核查这套系统能否在能见度不理想的条件下有效识别道路危险物。
据IT之家了解，无人驾驶出租车行业的领头羊 Waymo 采用了一套和特斯拉不一样的方案：激光雷达（LiDAR），依靠激光光束扫描周边环境。不过去年的一个深夜，一台 Waymo 车辆依旧撞死了一只名叫 Kit‑Kat 的 9 岁虎斑猫；这件事发生之后，周边不少居民纷纷发帖悼念这只小猫。
根据特斯拉向美国国家公路交通安全管理局提交的事故报告，2025 年 9 月，奥斯汀一台用于 Robotaxi 运营的特斯拉 Model Y 撞到了一只突然冲上马路的狗。事后这只狗自行跑开，看上去并没有受伤。
马斯克本人曾经养过猫，其中一只取名叫薛定谔（Schrödinger），名字源自物理学家那个著名的猫咪思想实验。马斯克曾经坦言，自己“努力试着去喜欢”薛定谔，但是“这只猫完全没有投桃报李，一丝好感都没有回馈给我。”
“后来有一天，它就消失不见了。”他说道。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 4 日消息，亚马逊云服务（AWS）首席执行官马特 · 加曼（Matt Garman）表示，在为新建数据中心项目争取审批的过程当中，该公司已经停止与政府机构签署保密协议（NDA）。
加曼的这句话出自一篇篇幅较长的官方博客。在这篇博文当中，他试图回应社会各界针对数据中心普遍存在的质疑，并且论证数据中心实际上能够为地方社区带来益处。
保密协议正是民众抵制数据中心建设浪潮当中的一大焦点问题。例如环保活动人士艾琳 · 布洛科维奇（Erin Brockovich）近期就提到，民众针对数据中心最多的投诉集中在透明度问题。这类项目往往存在一套共性模式：“项目拿到许可之后才对外公布；开发方拒不回复当地居民的电话咨询；地方官员在周边民众还完全不知情的情况下，就先行签署了保密协议。”
受民间反对声音的影响，纽约已经宣布暂停大型数据中心审批，为期一年。据加曼称，眼下美国各地还有超过 100 项关于暂停审批数据中心的提案正在审议当中。
加曼提出：“如果这类限制政策正式落地，美国相当于在这场（AI 算力）竞赛当中给自己开出一张落败的罚单，其影响将会延续好几代人。作为一个国家，我们承受不起这样的局面。”
此外，加曼还试图破除流传较广的四大关于数据中心的误区：耗水量过大、推高居民电价、造成巨量污染排放、无法给所在社区带来收益。
他引用亚马逊自家的用水报告指出，“数据中心直接耗水量”仅占美国全部工业用水消耗量的 0.5%，“比高尔夫球场、扁桃种植以及许多其他行业低好几个数量级”。
英伟达此前曾宣称自家全新冷却系统几乎可以消除数据中心内部全部用水。然而和亚马逊的说辞类似，这类说法似乎忽略了发电以及芯片制造环节背后更广范围的水资源消耗。科研人员也表示，他们需要独立研究数据中心的水与能源消耗；目前无论是联邦还是各州层面，都没有强制科技企业上报相关数据的法规。
针对电价问题，加曼表示，只有部分建有大量数据中心的州出现电价上涨；另一些地区电价有所下降，或者至少涨幅更为平缓。他同时提出观点：“在电价上涨的部分地区，主要根源在于电网设施老旧；在新增算力需求到来之前，当地就缺少投资扩建。”
但与之相对，一家独立监督机构近期发布的看法是，在美国规模最大的电网体系当中，数据中心正是电价同比大涨 76% 的主要诱因。
至于污染排放问题 —— 美国全国有色人种协进会（NAACP）目前正就此起诉埃隆 · 马斯克旗下的 SpaceX 与 xAI。加曼抱怨，批评者总是拿数据中心许可文件上面写明的最大允许排放值说事。举个例子，亚马逊计划落地于得克萨斯州的一处数据中心，许可的二氧化碳年排放上限为 3300 万吨，该数值超过美国境内任何一座发电厂。
“但事实是，数据中心的备用发电机组几乎不会实际启动运行。”加曼写道，“发电机组 99.9% 的时间都处于闲置状态（每年大约仅运行 10 小时，大多只是开展强制性维护测试）。”
谈及社区收益这一部分，加曼明确写道：“我们在项目合作当中，已经不再和各级政府机构签署保密协议。”除此之外他还补充：“过去三年，亚马逊已经向国内建有重要数据中心的各地社区累计投入超过 10 亿美元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 67.2 亿元人民币）。”

这样的表态是否足以打消地方民众的疑虑？或许还远远不够。Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥 · 阿莫迪（Dario Amodei）近期提出，当下社会对于 AI 的抵制本质上属于一场信任危机。民众普遍认为政府与科技企业总是“想方设法琢磨出新的法子损害普通人的利益”。与此类似，撰稿人贾斯敏 · 孙（Jasmine Sun）也提到，当反对建设数据中心的居民听完科技企业的解释之后，他们的反应往往依旧是：“我不相信他们。”

cards.summary: 【Hugging Face 官方动态】The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.
fulltext: Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.
A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.
Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”
Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.
An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.
Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.
A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:
Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.
We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.
One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.
Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.
The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.
Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.
Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.
Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.
If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.
Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:
Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)
This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.
Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.
A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.
Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.
Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.
Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20
Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.
Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.
Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:
These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.
Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.
ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.
Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.
The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.
In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:
In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.
Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:
Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.
Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.
The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

fulltext_cn: 图1 ： ThinkingBox针对孤立的MCP工具会话运行代理，然后对终端后端状态及其留下的副作用进行评分。来自我们的ThinkingBox论文。
一位顾客来信。她的$ 745厨房电器在纳什维尔配送中心被困在快递“例外”中，比预计交货日期晚了15天。
人工智能代理小心翼翼地工作。九个工具调用：提取订单、检查跟踪、查找客户个人资料、两次搜索退款政策、确认不存在工单、打开工单、记录时间表并正确阅读政策；她的账号部分确实不符合延迟交付补偿的资格。
然后，系统会在工单解决后关闭工单，并回复「由于您的问题已解决，有什么我可以帮忙的吗？」
有两件事是错的。承运人异常仍处于打开状态，因此所需的结束状态暂停，等待解决。客户从未得到她实际要求的真正答案。
人工智能分级机检查工具调用将看到九个格式良好的调用。评分员检查代理是否写入数据库也会看到这一点。数据库有不同意见。
这一差距正是ThinkingBox所衡量的。在507个有状态的业务工作流程中，每个工作流针对各种LLM模型运行20次，它根据终端后端状态和副作用对代理进行评级。本文介绍了我们的发现、一致性成本以及如何通过OpenEnv自行运行基准。
您可以自己运行：上面的示例改编自基准任务sandbox_external_retail_group1.py: test_case_ST003_006 ，失败的可执行文件检查是单个字段：工单的状态在要求的结束状态保持时得到解决。完整的痕迹在我们论文的附录D.4案例3中。
想在阅读结果之前尝试一下吗？跳到“自己运行”部分。
最终响应和有效的工具调用仅为代理。客服代表在留下错误值、更改错误记录或产生额外副作用时，听起来可能是正确的。只有它留下的记录才能解决问题。
差距很大。在一项涵盖12个LLM模型的121,680项有效试验的常见消融中， 79,853次尝试未通过可执行检查。在这些故障中， 67.24 ％仍然干净利落地终止，调用了状态更改工具，并且没有报告最终工具错误。然而，可执行检查发现其中77.61%的字段值错误， 43.30%的字段值意外的额外影响， 25.36%的字段值缺失。这些状态检查结果相互重叠。
轨迹是一种宣称。数据库状态是证据。重复是信任测试。
专员正确处理一次退款，并在接下来的四次处理不当，这不是正常工作的退款专员。因此，每个任务运行20次，每次都来自相同的干净后端，我们报告三种不同的事情：
表1 ：我们报告的三个数字，以及每个问题的答案。
我们使用这篇博客文章中观察到的20/20作为507项任务中有多少项在20项中通过了20项的字面计数。没有估算器，没有平滑。
从熟悉的视角开始。下表按域分列了单次尝试得分估算值PASS @ 1。这是大多数排行榜发布的数字，它本身就像一个普通的能力排名。
表2 ：按域划分的ThinkingBox-Bench通过@ 1 (%)。对每个任务的每个模型进行20次重复试验的评估。粗体标记组长；下划线标记亚军。我们的ThinkingBox论文中的表4提供了单次尝试分数估计的标准误差。
克劳德作品5.5以67.16%的总体领先，比克劳德作品5高出三分之二。Kimi-K3是GPT-6-Astra点内最强的开放式重量模型。域名同样重要： Claude Opus 4.6的零售得分为68.62% ，汽车保险得分为8.30%。
一次良好的运行可以告诉你模型可以完成这项工作。它不会告诉你它是否会再次这样做。因此，运行每项任务20次，并询问该分数中有多少幸存下来。
图2 ：每个模型的单次尝试得分在20次重复中存活了多少。
只有三个人在1分时保留了大部分分数： GPT-6 Astra保留了78%的单次尝试率，而Claude Opus 5.5和Claude Opus 5各保留了71%。另一方面， GLM-5.1、Kimi-K2.6和DeepSeek-V4-Pro各占8%左右。
模型一次可以做什么和每次都可以做什么之间的差距就是整个故事。
图3 ：宽度和一致性拉开。显示了十八个型号中的十二个；为便于阅读，省略了六个低于33 ％合格@ 1的型号。
Kimi-K3在我们测试的任何型号中都有最广泛的覆盖范围。它至少一次解决了93.89%的基准： 507项任务中的476项。只有31个任务完全击败它，这是该领域的最低计数。在零售工作流程中，它以82.24% @ 1的成绩领先，领先于所有专有模式。
Kimi-K3也是一致性最低的之一。在507项任务中，只有68项（ 13.41% ）在20次尝试中都取得了成功。
克劳德作品5颠倒了这一点。它至少解决一次较少的任务（ 79.09 ％; 106完全击败它） ，但每次尝试完成47.53 ％的基准。
新型号并没有解决这个问题。Claude Opus 5.5 的每次尝试平均得分都高于 Claude Opus 5（67.16% 对 66.50%），并且至少能解决更多题目。在所有 20 次尝试中，它通过的题目数量完全相同：241 道。仅仅提高了 0.5 个百分点的准确率，并没有带来任何可靠性上的提升。
如果您正在为接触真实记录的工作选择模型，则PASS @ 20是不适合查看的列。
能力比较通常停留在分数上。对于任何部署的人来说，相关的问题是一个成功的工作单位的成本。我们将其作为每次成功任务尝试的成本来衡量。我们称之为任务尝试，因为每个基准任务都会重复运行，并且每次尝试都会产生成本，因此PASS @ 1是匹配的质量分母。
我们从其完整的507 × 20活动中获取了每个模型的记录代币使用情况，并以OpenRouter +上可用的未贴现价目表价格对其进行了定价，从而取消了促销折扣，并排除了声明量化的端点。输入、输出和缓存速率都来自每个模型的一个提供程序端点。
然后，我们将一次运行的成本除以成功的尝试次数：
每次成功任务尝试的成本= 507次尝试的估计成本，每次任务一次÷ (507 × pass @ 1)
这是一个比较效率指数，不是发票，也不是满足一个生产请求的价格。它还对单一成功进行定价，而不是一致性。接下来是我们的价格一致性。
示例： GPT-5.4每507次尝试（每项任务一次尝试）花费43.49美元，并且在1次尝试中通过了65.36% ，因此每次成功的任务尝试花费43.49美元÷ （ 507 × 0.6536 ） = 0.131美元。
如果没有其他模型既不昂贵又至少准确，那么模型就在前沿。三个型号合格；其他所有型号至少在一个轴上占主导地位。
图4 ：针对PASS @ 1的每次成功任务尝试的成本。环形圆点是帕累托成本前沿模型。
边界有三个步骤。GPT-5.6 SOL的每次成功成本最低，为$ 0.127 ； GPT-5.4每次成功增加$ 0.004 ，可将PASS @ 1提高3.45个百分点； Claude Opus 5.5每次成功增加$ 0.276 ，可再增加1.80个百分点。由于没有更便宜的型号与其通行证@ 1相匹配，因此三者中的每一个都保持在成本前沿线上。
Claude Opus 5是最明显的例子：每次成功尝试$ 0.475 ，通过率为66.50% @ 1 ，比Claude Opus 5.5的$ 0.276和67.16%更昂贵，准确率更低。
每次成功的成本奖励一个便宜且通常正确的模型。它不会奖励每次都正确的模型。因此，我们还计算了每个可靠任务的成本：整个20次营销活动的成本除以模型在所有20次尝试中传递的任务数。
每项可靠任务的成本= 20次507次尝试的估计成本÷超过20/20的任务
示例：活动的GPT-6-Astra成本为20 × $ 86.03 = $ 1,720.60 ，每次尝试通过231个任务，因此每个可靠任务的GPT-6-Astra成本为$ 1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $ 7.45。
表3 ：在具有至少一个观察到的20/20任务的模型中，每个可靠任务的九个最低成本，从低到高排序。预估$ ，而不是实际的云账单。
现在按一致性排名。GPT-5.4最便宜，价格为6.80 $ ，但只有128项任务符合标准。GPT-6 Astra达到231 ，价格为$ 7.45 ， Claude Opus 5.5是联合最高的241 ，价格为$ 7.80。
这三者都不能主宰其他任务：每项额外的可靠任务都会花费更多。克劳德作品5也超过了241 ，但价格为13.30 $ ，因此作品5.5完全占据主导地位。GPT-5.6 SOL ，每次成功最便宜，为$ 0.127 ，每项可靠任务的成本为$ 9.76。获得正确答案的最便宜方法不是获得可靠答案的最便宜方法。
我们为每个失败的跟踪分配一个确定性诊断签名，标题是可操作的：大约五分之四的失败是工具处理，而不是推理。在我们论文表5中的一项消融研究中：
这些是每个模型份额和可观察标签的未加权平均值，而不是独特的因果解释。
实际模式很简单：代理通常会尝试工作流程，然后无法从工具错误、失败的前提条件或空查找中恢复。这是一个重试和错误恢复问题，然后才是模型问题。
难度也随领域而变化：在上表2中列出的模型中，零售平均合格率为59.52% @ 1 ，而汽车保险平均合格率为33.83%。
该怎么办。将20/20速率视为设计输入，而不是判决。基准成绩在生产中可用的相同信号：在提交之前检查终端状态，而不是模型的总结。
对工具和系统错误进行分类，以便重试针对可恢复的错误。将工具表面切割为工作流程所需的内容。并且需要人工批准您无法廉价逆转的变更。我们还没有在这个基准上测量其中任何一个的升力，这正是环境现在可以测试的东西。
ThinkingBox是代理沙箱，而ThinkingBox-Bench是评估代理的数据集基准。这篇文章顶部的图表显示了循环；这是每个部分的作用。
图5 ：上图1中面板A的沙盒循环：隔离工具会话、终端数据库状态、副作用、可执行文件判断。
每个任务定义起始后端状态、用户目标、可用的MCP工具、域策略和终端状态的可执行检查。模拟用户持有私人信息（预订推荐语、偏好或出生日期） ，只有在被要求时才会释放。

fulltext: During a presentation on the future of RE Engine, Capcom laid out its plans to embrace AI in ‘development workflows.’

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail and Google Calendar, with support for Outlook and Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and cancelling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls.
The company remains in private beta.

Powered by Hermes agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details, flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.
Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.
It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text.
Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard.
Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages.
Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.
Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.
Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.
There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes.

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.
Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.
Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.
The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.
The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.
The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.
In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.
Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.
Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.
Fo launched publicly in September 2025 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

它包括一个免费的基本选项，但也提供基于家庭规模的不同订阅，起价为每月$ 9.99。
与其他以家庭为重点的代理类似， Ollie背后的想法是，家庭已经拥有他们需要的信息，但它存在于学校信息、日历、任务列表和群聊中。Ollie的目标是将这些碎片整合在一起并保持同步。它可以跟踪日历、电子邮件、提醒、任务和其他家庭详细信息，然后通过短信向用户提供相关信息。
它与其他代理商的最大区别在于， Ollie是首批实现SOC 2合规性（一种广泛使用的安全标准）的主流、以家庭为中心的人工智能助手之一。
Ollie于2026年6月推出，提供免费会员等级，以及每月$ 25起150条消息的付费套餐。每月$ 100的方案最多包含1,000条消息。
Orbits还有一个专注于家庭的人工智能助手。
它通过Orbits应用程序和短信工作，可以将日历、列表和对话汇集在一起，同时还为您执行任务。这可能包括搜索网页、购物、预订餐厅、更改预约以及请求家庭服务报价。
此外， Orbits还可以提醒家庭成员做家务，与服务提供商沟通，并帮助协调直系亲属以外的责任。
Orbits得到了Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun基金、N49P和Garage Capital等投资者的支持。
用户可以像与朋友一样与Pally互动，同时可以访问他们已经依赖的应用程序。该助手可以连接分布在WhatsApp、Gmail、日历和Google云端硬盘等服务中的信息，帮助用户跟踪计划、收据、日期、文件和其他详细信息。
有免费套餐，提供每月15分钟通话等功能，也有付费套餐，包括30分钟通话每月25美元， 60分钟每月100美元。
Poke于2026年3月推出，作为通用助手，您可以通过短信联系到。它可以处理涉及日历、规划、健康和健身、智能家居控制、照片和其他日常活动的任务。
Poke在2026年6月变得特别引人注目，当时苹果批准Poke成为Apple Messages for Business平台上的第一个人工智能代理。一个月后，母公司The Interaction Company of California被人工智能编程初创公司Cognition收购，交易价值低至九位数。
Rene是一个人工智能个人助理，旨在成为用户的“最佳联系人” ，而不是另一个生产力代理。它基于文本，可以将自然语言对话转化为任务、提醒、摘要和其他后续行动。Rene还在对话中保持语境，使其能够记住细节，并展示以后可能需要注意的事情。
此外，它有一个浏览器，可以编写代码，为您购物，以及创建幻灯片和图像。
Rene目前可在iMessage、Telegram和WhatsApp上使用。
Skye不是等待用户打开应用程序，而是iPhone的“代理主屏幕” ，它分析来自连接服务的信息，并通过上下文卡片、建议和每日简报显示其认为相关的信息。助理可以生成音频简报，在会议前准备信息，表面提醒，并确定潜在的有用信息。
该公司Signull Labs在2025年筹集了约360万美元的种子资金。它于2026年4月进入私人测试和测试版，尚未公布公开发布日期。
Stanley是一名针对内容创作者而非一般个人生产力的人工智能内容助理。它通过iMessage、Telegram和网络提供，充当内容的AI负责人，帮助用户提出想法，将其转化为帖子，并保持一致的发布时间表。
例如， Stanley可以连接到用户的Instagram账号，使用该上下文根据用户的实际行为推荐内容。用户还可以发送语音笔记， Stanley会将其转换为脚本、字幕和其他社交资产。它包括一个内容日历，可以安排帖子，其更广泛的目标是使内容创建成为一个更连续、更自动化的流程，而不是用户必须坐下来从头开始计划。
与Tomo的iMessage个人助理的最大区别在于， Tomo可以成为小组对话的一部分，而不是只与您互动的私人助理。
此外，与其他客服代表一样，它旨在帮助实现目标、问责制、日程安排和日常组织。它还可以发送提醒、搜索网页、处理日历和电子邮件、观看视频和编辑照片。
基本套餐起价为每月$ 19.99。
Town更注重职业生活。它为用户提供了一个“Townie” ，这是一个人工智能助手，旨在了解他们的工作方式并处理反复出现的专业任务。它可以与电子邮件、日历、文档、Slack和其他平台配合使用。
2026年6月，该公司筹集了由Andreessen Horowitz和Forerunner牵头的5500万美元A轮融资。

该系列前两部《灵魂摆渡·蝴蝶梦》《灵魂摆渡·天女之梦》于8月22日独家上线爱奇艺，备受观众喜爱，上线首周即收回两部影片制作成本，首月累计分账票房突破800万元。随着第三部《灵魂摆渡·公主之梦》于10月1日上线，系列热度进一步攀升，带动影片热度和分账票房持续增长。截至10月3日，“浮生梦”系列累计分账票房突破1000万元。
作为经典IP“灵魂摆渡”的全新网络故事片系列化开发，“浮生梦”系列延续原作中式志怪、借鬼怪写人心的创作内核，并通过全新故事进一步拓展人物前史与IP世界观。
三部作品分别从不同故事切入，逐步揭开“灵摆铁三角”赵吏、夏冬青、娅的前世今生与命运轨迹。《灵魂摆渡·蝴蝶梦》围绕庄周梦蝶的东方哲学意象展开；《灵魂摆渡·天女之梦》通过多重梦境探寻命运抉择与人生真谛；《灵魂摆渡·公主之梦》则透过一桩离奇案件牵出一段尘封百年的守候与执念，三位摆渡人的故事也由此持续展开。
上线以来，《灵魂摆渡》“浮生梦”系列持续收获观众关注与好评。社交平台上，不少新老剧粉围绕剧情细节、人物前史及系列伏笔展开讨论。观众对经典角色的情感共鸣，以及对后续故事的期待，也持续推动该系列网络故事片热度走高。
《灵魂摆渡》“浮生梦”系列的连续推出，也展现了AIGC技术在经典IP内容开发中的应用潜力。一方面，依托AIGC制作方式，作品能够以更灵活、高效和更具性价比的方式，呈现奇幻、志怪等具有较高视觉想象空间的场景，为经典IP拓展新的视觉表达。另一方面，通过“AI技术+真人表演迁移”的创作方式，作品得以突破角色年龄和线性时间等限制，经典角色能够进入新的故事与叙事时空，IP系列化延展获得更多可能。
与此同时，三部作品在制作过程中还沉淀了近500个角色资产、近800个场景资产，以及近200个核心道具资产。这些数字资产可复用于后续内容开发，在保持人物形象与表演风格统一的同时，进一步提升IP开发的生产效率和制作灵活性。
9月23日，在爱奇艺iJOY秋季悦享会上，爱奇艺创始人、CEO龚宇表示，过去三四个月，实拍内容中AI开始“爆发性地应用”，显著提升视听体验、缩短制作周期、降低成本。他同时强调，AI是内容的加分项，不是用来搭建流水线、生产工业化、标准化产品的工具，不能牺牲内容品质。
从《灵魂摆渡》“浮生梦”系列的观众口碑和商业表现看，该系列作品正是实现了以AI技术拓展表达边界、以品质叙事回应观众期待，充分展现出AIGC在制作效率、数字资产沉淀及商业回报等方面的应用价值，也为AIGC影视内容从技术探索走向系列化品质创作、收获商业回报提供了可参考的路径。

cards.title: What’s the best Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 series chip? I tested them all to find out
cards.title_cn: 最好的Snapdragon 8 Gen 5系列芯片是什么？我对它们进行了全部测试，以了解
cards.summary: 【Android Authority】Credit: Tushar Mehta / Android Authority The Snapdragon 8 series is Qualcomm’s top-tier of smartphone processors. These chips offer a ton of performance, blazing-fast connectivity, cutting-edge camera…
fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

The Snapdragon 8 series is Qualcomm’s top-tier of smartphone processors. These chips offer a ton of performance, blazing-fast connectivity, cutting-edge camera features, and loads of AI features. This family grew in a big way in 2026, though. And that’s before we talk about the brand new Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series.

We already saw the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 in late 2025, but then we got the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V. So, which one is best? Well, we’ve now tested phones with all of these Gen 5 chips. And we have an answer. For these tests, we used the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, POCO F9 Ultra, POCO F9 Pro, and the OnePlus 15R.
The results below are… interesting.

The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, seen in the POCO F9 Ultra, is the best Snapdragon chip that most Android OEMs can buy. Expect an octa-core 4.6GHz Oryon CPU and a powerful Adreno GPU with three compute slices. However, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, used in the Galaxy S26 Ultra, is effectively an overclocked version for Samsung devices. Its CPU reaches an impressive peak speed of 4.74GHz. Unfortunately, this chipset is typically restricted to Samsung. In saying so, Qualcomm tends to release small quantities of its overclocked chips to other OEMs in the second half of each year under the “Leading Version” moniker.

The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V used in the POCO F9 Pro is the latest Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip, and it’s essentially a downgraded version of the 8 Elite Gen 5. The GPU, in particular, has only two compute slices, suggesting reduced peak performance. Otherwise, it still has the same 4.6GHz CPU and 3nm TSMC design as the full-fledged Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.

At the bottom of the totem pole is the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, seen in the OnePlus 15R. Notice the missing “Elite” branding? It uses a CPU similar to the Elite chip but reaches a top speed of 3.8 GHz. Furthermore, the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 has an Adreno GPU with two slices. It also lacks the high-performance memory that’s attached to the 8 Elite Gen 5 GPU. This suggests a significant graphical disadvantage on paper.

It’s no surprise to see the Galaxy S26 Ultra come out on top in both single- and multi-core CPU performance in our GeekBench 6 test. After all, the Ultra phone is equipped with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chipset. This processor has Prime CPU cores that are ~140MHz faster than the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V cores. It’s a narrow win in the single-core test, but the gap widens in the multi-core benchmark as Samsung can call on two higher-clocked cores.
Unsurprisingly, the OnePlus 15R came dead last in both legs of our GeekBench 6 test. This is at least partially due to the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5’s slower clock speeds across the board.

What is perhaps unexpected is that the POCO F9 Pro and its Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V ranked a distant third. Qualcomm previously noted that this processor had the same CPU clock speed and core count as the full-blown 8 Elite Gen 5. It therefore stands to reason that the chipset either has a smaller cache or POCO went with very conservative software tuning on the Pro compared to the Ultra.

GPU stress tests aren’t necessarily indicative of real-world performance. Furthermore, smartphones often vary greatly in their default power profiles and hardware cooling measures. Nevertheless, these benchmarks can still tell us which phones and chips might struggle under sustained load.

The Wild Life Stress Test and Wild Life Extreme Stress Test yield similar results upon close inspection. The POCO F9 Pro achieves the best stability of the lot at ~76-77% across both tests. Meanwhile, the POCO F9 Ultra offered 69-70% stability, and the Galaxy S26 Ultra maintained just 53-54% stability. The POCO F9 Pro’s performance means that it started out behind the Galaxy S26 Ultra in both tests, but finished ahead of it by the end. The OnePlus 15R was last in both stress tests, but maintained 64-65% stability. This means that while the Samsung phone finished higher in both tests, the OnePlus device lost less performance over time.

We see a major shake-up in device temperatures, though. The POCO F9 Ultra achieved the highest temperatures across both tests. More specifically, you’re looking at average temperatures of 44-45 degrees Celsius and peak temperatures of 52 degrees Celsius. Xiaomi’s Pro phone wasn’t much better, with an average temperature of 43 degrees Celsius and a peak temperature of 50 degrees Celsius in both tests. That’s not great for your comfort or for either phone’s battery.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra was clearly cooler than the POCO phones. It achieved an average temperature of 41 degrees Celsius across both tests and a peak of 44 degrees Celsius. In other words, the Samsung phone’s peak temperatures are in line with the POCO F9 Ultra’s average temperature. That’s an interesting result and suggests that Samsung is a little more willing to drop performance in the name of lower temperatures.

The big winner in this regard was the OnePlus 15R, which had average temperatures of 34-35 degrees Celsius and a peak temperature of 41 degrees Celsius. Yep, this phone’s peak temperature is actually lower than the POCO duo’s average temperature. The sustained performance is still some way off the POCO phones, but at least the device won’t be uncomfortable to hold during long gaming sessions.

We have to reiterate that this isn’t a definitive verdict regarding each chip’s performance. Hardware cooling can play a major role in how a chip performs. Even software tuning can vary wildly from one OEM to another. So it’s entirely possible that a different set of phones running these same chips could see different results. However, there are some conclusions we can draw from our testing.

Based purely on CPU performance, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy is the best Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 series chip of the lot. By contrast, the OnePlus 15R and its non-Elite chip are dead-last. All of these chips have powerful CPUs that should keep your phone running smoothly, though. However, the Galaxy chip’s increased performance could make a minor difference for tasks like video editing, bleeding-edge emulation, or running unoptimized AI models.

It’s much harder to pick a winner when looking at the GPU benchmarks. POCO’s phones clearly do the best job of maintaining performance over time, but these are also the hottest devices of the lot. Samsung’s phone loses the most performance and even finishes behind the POCO F9 Pro (with its downgraded GPU), but it’s a little cooler than Xiaomi’s devices.

Then there’s the OnePlus 15R. It’s in third place for stability and doesn’t threaten any of these phones’ overall performance. However, it’s far and away the coolest phone of the lot while still bringing plenty of performance compared to upper-mid-range devices. This makes it the ideal pick in my book for comfortably playing blockbuster Android games or mid-tier emulation (e.g., PS2 and Nintendo Switch).

fulltext_cn: Android Authority上的会员链接可能会为我们赚取佣金。了解详情。
2026年10月3日—美国东部时间上午6:00
Snapdragon 8系列是高通公司的顶级智能手机处理器。这些芯片提供了大量的性能、超快的连接性、尖端的摄像头功能和大量的人工智能功能。不过，这个家庭在2026年有了很大的发展。这是在我们谈论全新的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6系列之前。

我们已经在2025年底看到了Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5和Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 ，但随后我们获得了用于Galaxy的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5和Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V。那么，哪一个是最好的？嗯，我们现在已经用所有这些第5代芯片测试了手机。我们有一个答案。在这些测试中，我们使用了三星Galaxy S26 Ultra、POCO F9 Ultra、POCO F9 Pro和一加15R。
下面的结果……很有趣。

在POCO F9 Ultra中看到的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5是大多数Android OEM可以购买的最好的Snapdragon芯片。预计八核4.6GHz Oryon CPU和具有三个计算片的强大Adreno GPU。然而， Galaxy S26 Ultra中使用的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy实际上是三星设备的超频版本。它的CPU达到了令人印象深刻的4.74 GHz峰值速度。不幸的是，此芯片组通常仅限于三星。这样说来，高通公司倾向于在每年下半年以“领先版本”的名义向其他原始设备制造商发布少量超频芯片。
POCO F9 Pro中使用的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V是最新的Snapdragon 8 Gen 5芯片，基本上是8 Elite Gen 5的降级版本。特别是GPU只有两个计算切片，这表明峰值性能降低。否则，它仍然具有与成熟的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5相同的4.6GHz CPU和3nm TSMC设计。
图腾柱的底部是一加15R中看到的Snapdragon 8 Gen 5。注意到缺少“精英”品牌吗？它使用与Elite芯片类似的CPU ，但最高速度可达3.8 GHz。此外， Snapdragon 8 Gen 5具有带有两个切片的Adreno GPU。它还缺少连接到8 Elite Gen 5 GPU的高性能内存。这表明纸上存在明显的图形缺陷。

在我们的GeekBench 6测试中， Galaxy S26 Ultra在单核和多核CPU性能方面都名列前茅，这并不奇怪。毕竟， Ultra手机配备了适用于Galaxy芯片组的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5。这款处理器的Prime CPU内核比Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5和Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V内核快约140MHz。在单核测试中，这是一个微弱的胜利，但随着三星可以调用两个更高时钟的核心，多核基准的差距扩大了。
不出所料，OnePlus 15R 在我们的 GeekBench 6 测试中两项测试均垫底。这至少部分是由于骁龙 8 Gen 5 处理器的全频运行速度较慢所致。
也许出乎意料的是， POCO F9 Pro及其Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5V排名第三。高通此前曾指出，这款处理器的CPU时钟速度和内核数量与成熟的8 Elite Gen 5相同。因此，与Ultra相比，芯片组要么具有较小的缓存，要么POCO在Pro上进行了非常保守的软件调优，这是有道理的。
GPU压力测试不一定表明真实世界的性能。此外，智能手机的默认电源配置和硬件冷却措施通常差异很大。尽管如此，这些基准仍然可以告诉我们哪些手机和芯片在持续负载下可能会遇到困难。

野生动物压力测试和野生动物极限压力测试在仔细检查后得出类似的结果。POCO F9 Pro在两次测试中都达到了批次的最佳稳定性，约为76-77%。与此同时， POCO F9 Ultra提供69-70%的稳定性，而Galaxy S26 Ultra仅保持53-54%的稳定性。POCO F9 Pro的性能意味着它在两次测试中都落后于Galaxy S26 Ultra ，但最终提前完成。OnePlus 15R在两次压力测试中都是最后一款，但稳定性保持在64-65%。这意味着，虽然三星手机在两次测试中的成绩都较高，但随着时间的推移， OnePlus设备的性能损失较少。
不过，我们看到设备温度发生了重大变化。POCO F9 Ultra在两次测试中都达到了最高温度。更具体地说，您看到的平均温度为44-45摄氏度，峰值温度为52摄氏度。小米的Pro手机也没有好多少，两次测试的平均温度都是43摄氏度，峰值温度都是50摄氏度。这不利于您的舒适性，也不利于任何一款手机的电池。
三星Galaxy S26 Ultra显然比POCO手机更酷。两次测试的平均温度均为41摄氏度，峰值为44摄氏度。换句话说，三星手机的峰值温度与POCO F9 Ultra的平均温度一致。这是一个有趣的结果，表明三星更愿意以较低的温度为名降低性能。
在这方面，最大的赢家是 OnePlus 15R，它的平均温度在 34-35 摄氏度之间，最高温度为 41 摄​​氏度。没错，这款手机的最高温度甚至比 POCO 双雄的平均温度还要低。虽然持续性能方面与 POCO 手机还有一定差距，但至少长时间玩游戏时握持感不会不舒服。
我们必须重申，这并不是对每个芯片性能的最终决定。硬件冷却可以在芯片的性能中发挥重要作用。即使是软件调优也可能因原始设备制造商而异。因此，运行相同芯片的不同手机完全有可能看到不同的结果。但是，我们可以从测试中得出一些结论。
纯粹基于CPU性能，适用于Galaxy的Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5是该批次中最好的Snapdragon 8 Gen 5系列芯片。相比之下，一加15R及其非精英芯片是永久性的。不过，所有这些芯片都具有强大的CPU ，可以让您的手机平稳运行。然而， Galaxy芯片的性能提升可能会对视频编辑、前沿模拟或运行未优化的AI模型等任务产生轻微影响。
在查看GPU基准时，选择获胜者要困难得多。POCO的手机显然在长期保持性能方面做得最好，但这些也是该系列中最热门的设备。三星的手机性能损失最大，甚至落后于POCO F9 Pro （ GPU降级） ，但它比小米的设备要酷一些。
还有OnePlus 15R。它在稳定性方面排名第三，不会威胁到这些手机的整体性能。然而，与中高端设备相比，它仍然是该系列中最酷的手机，同时仍然带来了充足的性能。这使它成为我书中舒适地玩大片Android游戏或中端模拟（例如， PS2和Nintendo Switch ）的理想选择。
感谢您成为我们社区的一员。发布前请阅读我们的评论政策。

cards.title: TDS REVIEW | CMF Clip Pro 耳夹式无线耳机体验
cards.title_cn: TDS评论| CMF Clip Pro 耳夹式无线耳机体验
cards.summary: 不知道以后 CMF 的设计还会不会像现在一样出彩。 查看全文
fulltext: 这篇文章是 TDS Studio 在少数派上的第 31 篇文章，依然是全平台首发。
Nothing 大体系下的第一个 OWS 产品其实是 Nothing Ear (Open)，我们其实也是首发期就入手了的，至少从精致程度以及调音的平衡性考虑，那还是个不错的产品，只是声音素质会跟千元价位当时的优秀档次状态有些差距而已。Clip Pro 则是他们的第一款耳夹，既然是 CMF 子品牌负责，显然设计语言和定位都会与主品牌有明显不同。考虑到它的售价，我们会以审视中档耳夹的角度来体验它。
CMF Clip Pro 的包装还是非常小巧的，也没有什么其他配件，开箱处有一如既往的胶贴，可以帮助你判断它是否是第一次启封。

Clip Pro 共有三种配色可选，似乎是去掉了在其他款式中常见的那个浅薄荷绿，耳夹这边保留了标志性的珊瑚橙色以及两种不同灰度的灰色。我们自然是挑了最具品牌气息的橙色款入手，它其实还是基于两种不同饱和度的橙色实现的。亮面部分比如充电盒内腔、耳机本体的前后模块都是饱和度更高的状态，盒外侧以及耳夹 C 桥部分是细磨砂处理或者亲肤硅胶层，相对会浅一点。这种珊瑚橙在大多数灯光下都有点三文鱼的感觉，并不会特别扎眼但还是足够鲜艳的。

充电盒整体非常小巧，不会比常规的 TWS 耳塞更大，顶盖上仍然保留了 CMF 耳塞产品的那个大旋钮，这也是通体唯一不是橙色的部分。这个旋钮正是耳机配对按键，以前 CMF 部分产品这个旋钮还可以实现其他功能，但目前在 Clip Pro 上默认是把旋转操作禁用的，在 app 端开启它之前，旋钮只是一个有段落感的解压玩具而已。同时或许是由于这个旋钮外露的比例比以前真无线产品更多，你在把玩旋转的时候会觉得它会出现倾斜，玩着玩着就卡一下，解压变增压……
USB 口位于背部，单手开盖还是非常轻松的，转轴虽然不是全金属，但反馈手感还算明确。耳机本体在盒内的放置方式有点怪，是后端模块朝下的交叉排布，如果你见过 FreeClip 2 的那种放置状态应该就会明白。耳机本体是分左右的，我们实测左右调换也不可以充电（磁铁极性导致你都放不进去，但磁吸力度足够，不用担心细节。

耳机本体我称之为「罗锅化」的耳夹形态，大体上仍然是可以视为前后模块 + C 桥的结构，但 C 桥跟前腔之间的固定并非常见耳夹的样子，而是加上了一个角度，这让前腔看上去会进一步往内弯，出音口的位置也会往里，你可以理解为做了更对准耳道口的结构。后端模块是比较规矩的圆柱形，从某些角度看上去甚至像是以前那个「垃圾桶」形态的 Mac Pro…… 但仔细去看，与耳廓接触的部分还是有轻微的曲面下凹，并非没做贴合结构。
这套设计使得佩戴的友好程度其实还不错，你也不必担心它会有低价耳夹常见的 C 桥偏硬的情况，前后模块之间的夹力较轻，且由于 C 桥长度足够，即使是厚耳廓也不用特别担心舒适度。这种结构也方便你一次性就佩戴好它，不需要频繁调整佩戴角度。
耳机本体支持 IP54 防尘防泼溅，应对基本的小雨天气没有问题，充电盒也支持 IPX2（虽然官网写的是「防尘」但 IPX2 对应的其实是防水等级，或许是标注错误）。
Clip Pro 的操作全部依靠后端模块顶部的实体按键实现，这也算是某种物理盲操设计，可以实现对于单击、双击、长按以及点击后再长按的动作识别，默认的逻辑是单击播放控制、双击/三击切歌、长按控制音量，较为直观，除了单次按压以外的操作均可以自定义。按压反馈的灵敏度不必担心，毕竟是实体按键，但提示音在一些连击操作下会有一秒左右的迟滞。音量适中，佩戴识别功能是没有的。
Nothing X app 依然保持了耳机设置类 app 中较为直观的 UI 逻辑，提供了寻找耳机、固件更新、调音和设置自定义等功能。寻找耳机依然是基于耳机本体发出比较高音量的连续提示音实现，响度不算很高，在安静室内相对可用但咖啡厅之类的嘈杂环境就不太够了。关于各项声音相关功能我们会在后文单开一段介绍。
Clip Pro 搭载了单侧双麦克风、全机身共四颗麦克风，全部用于通话收音与降噪。我们实际在运营商网络下进行通话测试，它实际通话稳定性还不错，响度适中，清晰度中规中矩，会有比较明显的失真。在环境噪音较复杂或者风噪影响下，能听到比较明显的算法介入。三个方向的风源都不会产生明显的影响，硬要说的来自后方的风源会有更明显的介入痕迹，但总体上通话抗风噪的效果还是不错的。
作为少有支持 LDAC 的耳夹，我们自然是要依然对于它在两种模式下的信号进行主观测试。
信号优先/最佳效果模式连接标准测试设备 Xperia 1 V 的状态下，无论 WLAN 关闭还是开启的情况下，卡顿丢包情况都比较少。距离 7.5m 且隔承重墙的状态下也不会有卡顿的明显增加。超过 8m 的隔墙距离下才会出现丢包卡顿。
设备不变，切换至音质优先模式，则信号稳定范围来到隔墙 2m 以内、空旷 3m 以内。在 3~5m 的范围内虽然不断连不卡顿，但是会有丢包感，这个表现其实并不算出色。
在信号密集区域打开 LDAC 音质优先，卡顿丢包情况在手持手机行走的情况下时有出现，信号优先下则大多能够保持相对稳定的近场连接能力。日常使用或是非信号密集区域通勤时，建议信号优先/最佳效果，不建议切换到音质优先的高码率状态。
切换到 AAC 之后，无论 WLAN 开启与否，Xperia 1 V 与 iPhone 17 的测试结果都是足够稳定的，也能在保持相当距离的情况下确保信号流畅，在 10m 内的范围没什么问题，隔墙或更远就会有一定影响。
它也支持 Google Fast Pair 和 Windows Swift Pair，双设备连接与 LDAC 并不冲突。
延迟方面，它有独立的低延迟模式，且低延迟模式与 LDAC 没有冲突。实际感知上，无论是否开启低延迟、在以 LDAC 编解码器信号优先连接 Xperia 1 V 的状态，进行流媒体视频和本地视频观看，它的延迟都大概控制在正常语速少于半个字的程度，表现还可以。

续航方面，官方宣称单次连续播放时间 10h，搭配充电盒一共为 32.5h。它还有一个额外的长续航模式可选，并在此状态下总续航能来到 36h。个人经过标准流程测试下来，以 LDAC 编解码器连接 Sony Xperia 1 V，设置其他为默认，以 50% 音量连续播放流媒体音乐（Apple Music Lossless）、播客节目（小宇宙），仅耳机续航为 6 小时 46 分钟（三次标识满电状态下均值）。LDAC 功耗偏大，考虑到官方的测量条件可能为 AAC，且 AAC 连接下同等条件测试结果三次最低值也有 10 小时 37 分钟，可以认为符合甚至略微超过官方描述。
充电方面，我们依然进行了测试，它在初期可以一度达到接近 2W，后期则稳定在 0.4~0.5W， PD 支持没问题。
Clip Pro 搭载了直径 10.8mm 的 TPU + LCP 振膜动圈单元，支持的编码是 SBC / AAC / LDAC。搭载了被称为 Malleus Algorithm 的算法，其实就是动态补偿。
Nothing X app 里提供了非常多的声音相关功能，我们都快速过一下。
空间音频其实并非 Dolby Atmos 标准，而是单纯的「空间音效」，对于人声的结像进行模糊化，显得头中效应减少，混响增多，仅此而已，没有常开的必要。低音增强共有两档，实际即使开启到最高档也并不会有轰头的情况，这个低音增强更多像是满足低音量下的额外补偿，而非以往 Nothing 耳机的明显加能量。

均衡器提供了一个自定义档位和五个预设。自定义档位下是三个频率点 ±6 档的调节，显然不具备 Headphone (1) 上的高级 PEQ。五种预设里我个人会建议尝试「增强人声」，在室外环境使用时对于一些短视频或播客场景中的人声信息凸出有正面作用。漏音抑制模式的实现方式有点像我们之前在 LinkBuds Clip 上见到的，对于高频有非常明显的衰减，对于音乐聆听没有什么好处，但的确在减少漏音中的中高频（也是主要会让别人听到的频段）上有明显作用。你可以单独选择在通话时开启，这个设计很好。

考虑到漏音抑制模式的特性，我们还是基于不开启它的状态来评价对于 OWS 耳机来说颇为重要的实际声压和漏音控制表现，标准状态 AAC 连接 iPhone 17 对比，跟这段时间新测的耳夹保持一致从而控制输出增益的变量（兴戈圆气、达音科 LUNA 以及马上要测的 vivo 新品等）。将系统软件音量控制在 50%，正常佩戴。就我个人来说，标准模式此时的播放音量，在安静室内聆听大部分以当下 remaster 标准电平歌曲时会觉得能听到细节，但是明显是比日常听音音量要低的，也要比圆气和 LUNA 同样示数下有所不足。在连接 Xperia 1 V 的时候，同样系统显示 50 % 时会因为 Xperia 的蓝牙增益较高达到足够聆听的音量，iPhone 17 就得到 70% 以上才能接近类似水平。由于不同系统、不同设备、不同听力状态都会对于你进行判断产生干扰，这点还是要注意。
漏音方面，还是 iPhone 50% 音量为准下在 10cm 开外仅有轻微感知，15cm 开外几乎不可感。防漏音表现即使放到旗舰耳夹里也算相当不错的水平，这点表现还不错，但只是部分因为声压并不算大导致的……
基于 LDAC 编码连接 Xperia 1 V，关闭低音增强、空间音频和漏音抑制，均衡器为自定义清零状态。
低频量感适中，厚度适中，饱满度不算多。弹性表现中规中矩，下潜能力在中价位表现还可以。收放速度适中，保留的残响较少。氛围烘托的晕染感和浓郁度都不多。Clip Pro 的低频总体上依然是比较干净的，相较于小米耳夹和一些数码品牌的中价位出品，Clip Pro 的低频质感会更加自然一些，不会显得过于凌厉，这点是把控得不错。基音位于中下盘的乐器没有前倾问题。

中频，人声的距离稍近，但不至于贴脸，精致程度适中。对于人声的质感表现略优先于线条刻画，厚度适中，线条的突出程度不会有额外强调。对于男女声之间的倾向不算明显，适合于不过于粗或者不偏锐利的声线类型，相对还算普适。颗粒感有所打磨，大体上还是比较平顺的。音色有轻微的暖感，但并不影响判断，大体上不会有明显的抓耳强调。喉音位置比较标准，气声比例适中，相较于不少入门耳夹，在丰富度上稍好。口水声等的前凸有所控制（不是完全磨平），齿音也比较平顺，不会有明显的耐听度问题。人声频段的通透度还可以，不至于有不自然的偏亮。
乐器方面，大部分乐器的呈现都是质感略优先于线条的。弦乐器中，小提琴、吉他、中提琴等的拉拨弦稍有凸出，但抓耳感不会过分。大提琴的形体感比较细，在空间里比例不多。铜管类的气势感不算足，需要亮度的小号等有相对多一点的亮感。木管类的自然度还可以，空气感稍有一点突出。乐器的泛音不算多，听上去较为精致。打击乐器中，Kick 的存在感不强，Snare 收得稍快，镲片类有足够亮度但金属感和刺激度还是有所控制的。
高频总体亮度适中，不会有明显的尖峰，整体还算比较平滑。中高频过渡区域有一定的厚度，极高频的延伸能力表现中规中矩，跟旗舰耳夹普遍水平比起来会在极高频信息量上缺点东西，滚降稍快稍早。
声场的规模不算大，横纵向距离都不会拉得很远，边界感的弥散度也不算高。结合中规中矩的「高度感」，Clip Pro 呈现出的是比较规矩的扁椭球形空间。人声与乐器之间的分离度在这个价位还可以，整体感没什么问题。解析能力中规中矩，有轻度的「解析感」强调。动态一般，瞬态还不错。

CMF Clip Pro 作为产品的综合完成度其实还可以，保持了 CMF 作为 Nothing 子品牌在设计方面的一些优势，续航和佩戴体验等没有明显短板，声音大体上也在我们认为的合理区间，没有出现风格走向怪异的情况。不过，我们对于中价位的耳夹还是期望能够有更好的声压，在大多数移动设备 50% 难以满足安静环境听音响度需求的情况下，我们还是难以给它 V 级推荐，更何况在圆气、LUNA 这些声音上完成度明显更高的型号已经推出的前提下，它的优势会更少一些。虽然有高码率编码，但在音质优先的模式下连接稳定性还需要优化。好在，相较于部分手机品牌的耳夹，CMF 这边的溢价反倒显得克制一些了，甚至有的渠道能更低，这也是我们愿意给 IV 级评分的原因之一。
